newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Rexrodt plays down concerns over EU enlargement.
newsitem.headline: Rexrodt plays down concerns over EU enlargement.

text.p: German Economic Minister Gunter Rexrodt on Tuesday played down western concerns over the European Union's (EU) enlargement plans, saying new members from the east would provide the West with large export markets and cheap suppliers.
"In western Europe, the (potential EU membership) of central and eastern European countries is often misunderstood," Rexrodt told members of the German-Hungarian Industrial and Trade Chamber.
"Central and eastern Europe is (potentially) a larger export market than the U.S.," he said.
He added that limitations on trade between the potential new members and western Europe should be abolished.
"With protectionism, we would hinder these countries in developing their economies and our own companies to increase their exports."
German firms need cheap suppliers from central and eastern Europe, and also from Asia and Latin America, he added.

However, the EU needs a reform in its agricultural and structural policies and in the mechanism of its decision-making before enlargement, he said, adding that the negotiations about a new Union treaty in Amsterdam, eventually leading to enlargement, seemed to be going well.
"Everything goes on the right track towards closing the (EU countries') intergovernmental conference," he said.
Rexrodt said that Hungary was an example for the dynamic development of the region's economic ties with the west.
The volume of Germany's annual trade with Hungary has doubled since 1991 and totalled 16.3 billion marks ($9.4 billion) in 1996.

Hungary's Ministry of Industry, Trade and Tourism said in a statement that Hungary's exports to Germany rose in 1996 by 21.8 percent to $5.3 billion, while the imports from Germany increased by 11.6 percent to $5.1 billion.

Germany accounts for 32 percent of Hungary's total foreign trade, and 36 percent of Hungary's exports, while German companies has invested $4.9 billion in Hungary, representing about 34 percent of all foreign direct investments, it added.
Rexrodt told a news conference that not only large German companies invested in Hungary, but also a large number of small and medium-size enterprises.
He urged Hungarian companies to invest in the eastern part of Germany, and to set up joint ventures with German firms in third countries.

He added that cost competitiveness of Hungarian firms, and the expertise and trade relations of German companies promised high earnings in cooperation in selling machinery in less developed countries.
Rexrodt said Hungary's economic adjustment programme and reforms were likely to secure an early European Union membership for the country and said that Germany would support Hungary to reach that.
"Hungary can be regarded as a model in the region in the area of economic reforms and this can lead the country to becoming among the first who will join the European Union." ($ = 1.731 German Marks)
